single partition

This is another good point. It is recommended but not obligatory that you partition your hard disk.

Advantages: if you have just one partition shit can happen and fill up your entire hard drive, from bugs (once I had a X server bug that created HUGE log files on my home partition) to simple dumb stuff like downloading too many files (who has never filled up their entire drive at least once doing something like this...). And once your HD reaches 100% full you're pretty much fucked - you won't even be able to log in or log out, from my experience. That is fine if you know how to reboot in rescue mode or use a live CD to delete files, otherwise it could become a major problem.

Disadvantages: having multiple partitions means that partitions are limited in size - if /tmp (where temporary files are stored) has 1GB then that will be the limit, it won't be able to use those other 50GB that your home partition has free. This is obvious but it has some implications: Debian for example has set a /tmp too small for me one time and I couldn't load 1-hour long YouTube videos. Even today my /var partition did not have enough space to make a system upgrade... thankfully it only meant I had to do a two-step upgrade (it could have been a lot worse I guess).

Anyway go ahead and do a single partition at first but when before doing your next install read up a bit on it, there is lot of info on the Internet to read about Linux partitioning. Just so you have a reference here are some of my specs:

9GB / (root)
10GB /tmp
3GB /var (I would make it 6GB next time, maybe)

Of course I have a big-ish hard drive so I chose to give some extra space to these partitions to avoid headaches. Note that some installers (like Debian) will offer to partition your entire hard-drive (or entire free space) so you don't have to worry about choosing the details if you don't wanna.

Once I have chosen which Linux version I want to use for my main computer I will more than likely partition a fairly large section just for backup, currently just using an external. I'm not sure I will run a secondary version of Linux under a separate partition as of now. Although that could change if I find a version that works well with games, while another works better for the rest of the house.

You could do that also but depending on where your Windows partition is located physically in your disk it could result in a slightly slower system. It would be almost unnoticeable but it would be there and if you're planning on using the Linux system for years it wouldn't hurt to do a clean format.

I'm assuming you mean that there is a Windows partition and another partition for personal data because if you have only one partition then it would be the same as formatting the whole disk.

Also forget all of this if you are using a solid state disk because it doesn't read data in the same way traditional hard disks do - so it doesn't matter where your data is located physically.
